title: How hardening and tempering change steel
examples: Why do blacksmiths dip hot steel in water?
Why does steel turn blue when heated?

explain.say: Steel with enough carbon can be made very hard. A smith heats it until it glows bright red, around 800 degrees Celsius, then plunges it into water or oil. This sudden cooling, called quenching, traps carbon in a strained crystal called martensite: very hard, but brittle as glass.

draw.text: How hardening and tempering change steel

explain.say: So the steel is tempered: gently reheated to around 200 to 250 degrees. This relaxes some strain, trading a little hardness for toughness, and leaves a pale straw colour on polished steel, right for knife edges.
Tempering hotter, around 300 degrees, turns the surface blue. Blue-tempered steel is softer but springier, ideal for springs and screwdrivers that must flex without snapping.

So hardness and toughness are a trade-off, and the tempering temperature chooses the balance. Heating steel hotter still and cooling it very slowly, called annealing, makes it soft enough to cut and shape.

faq.a: Quenching is cooling hot steel very suddenly by plunging it into water, oil or brine. It gives the carbon atoms no time to move out of the way, freezing them into a hard, strained structure.
asks: Why do blacksmiths dip hot steel in water?

faq.a: Martensite is the crystal structure formed when carbon steel is quenched. Carbon atoms are trapped inside the iron crystals and distort them, making steel extremely hard but brittle.
asks: Why is quenched steel so hard?

faq.q: Why is tempering needed after hardening?
faq.a: Fully hardened steel is so brittle that a knock can shatter it. Tempering reheats it gently so some of the trapped strain relaxes, making the steel tougher while keeping most of its hardness.

faq.q: Why does steel change colour when heated?
faq.a: Heating polished steel grows a very thin layer of oxide on the surface. As it thickens, light reflecting from its top and bottom interferes, showing straw, brown, purple and blue. Smiths used these colours as a thermometer.
asks: Why does steel turn blue when heated?

faq.a: Annealing means heating steel and then cooling it very slowly, often inside the furnace. It removes hardness and stress, making the steel soft and easy to cut, bend or machine before it is hardened again.

facts: Temper colours come from a thin oxide film on the steel; pale straw appears at about 220 °C and blue at about 300 °C.
Quenching carbon steel forms martensite, a hard but brittle structure.

quiz.say: A smith wants a spring that bends without snapping. How should the quenched steel be tempered?

options.show: Not at all, to keep it hardest
options.say: Not at all, to keep it hardest

quiz.why: Blue tempering, around 300 °C, gives softer but tougher, springier steel.

wrong.1: Untempered quenched steel is brittle and would snap.
wrong.2: Melting would undo all the shaping and treatment.
